title: Generative Antibody and Protein Design
answer: Generative models now propose antibodies and proteins that have never existed, and some companies report double digit experimental hit rates for fully de novo designs, far above traditional screening. Venture money has followed: Chai Discovery raised $70 million in August 2025 and $130 million in December 2025.

reading.body:
Generative protein design is producing real experimental results and real money, but the reported hit rates are the designers' own numbers, not independent ones.

The pattern is a reversal of how antibody discovery has worked. Instead of immunising animals or screening large libraries and optimising whatever turns up, a model is given a target and proposes sequences predicted to bind it, with properties like stability or low immunogenicity built in. De novo means no starting antibody at all. Companies report double digit experimental hit rates for these designs, which is far above traditional screening, and the first generatively engineered antibody has reached a phase 3 trial. Chai Discovery's two raises, $70 million in August 2025 and $130 million in December 2025, show investors pricing that claim.

For AI specifically, the significance is that the model is doing the proposing rather than the sorting. That shifts the bottleneck. A lab can only test so many designs, so a higher hit rate means fewer wet lab cycles per candidate, and the compute spent generating sequences substitutes for bench work spent filtering them. The phase 3 entry matters more than any hit rate, because it is the first evidence in this data that a designed molecule survived the conventional development that follows design.

What the data does not cover is whether these hit rates hold on targets the designing company did not choose. It also says nothing about safety, manufacturing, or trial outcomes beyond the fact that one trial started. A hit rate measures binding in a lab assay. It does not measure whether a binder becomes a medicine, and the source of every reported figure here is the company making the claim.

The mechanism that separates generative design from screening is where the search happens. Screening searches a physical library that already exists, so its ceiling is set by how many molecules a lab can hold and assay. A generative model searches a learned distribution and can propose sequences that were never in any library, which is why it can address targets that conventional methods struggle to hit. The practical consequence is that the binding problem becomes a generation problem, and the cost of a candidate shifts from bench time toward compute time.

The data supports one comparison and it is not between hit rates. It is between a claim and an outcome. Double digit hit rates and two venture rounds are both statements about the design step. The phase 3 trial of GB-0895 is the only item in this data that speaks to what happens after design, and it is the only one that required anyone outside the designing company to agree. A hit rate is measured by the party that built the model. A trial start is registered by a party with no stake in the model's reputation.

That asymmetry sets the practical rule for a research team. Prospective results on blinded targets are the only form of evidence that tests whether a model generalises beyond the targets its designers chose, and the data here contains no such results. Everything reported is retrospective and self-selected.

What is a hit rate?

The share of designed molecules that show the desired activity, such as binding the target, when tested in the lab. It is a laboratory assay measurement, not a measure of whether the molecule works as a medicine.

Is a de novo antibody a drug?

Not yet. It is a starting point that still needs optimisation, safety testing, manufacturing development and trials. The data records one generatively engineered antibody, GB-0895, entering a phase 3 trial, which is the furthest any design in this data has progressed.

How much did Chai Discovery raise?

$70 million in a Series A announced in August 2025 and $130 million in a Series B announced in December 2025. The Series B announcement cited double digit experimental hit rates for de novo antibody design.

Do the reported hit rates come from independent testing?

No. The data attributes them to the companies making the claim, and the Series B figure is cited in Chai Discovery's own funding announcement. The data contains no third party replication of any hit rate.

Have any designed antibodies reached late stage trials?

Yes, one. Generate:Biomedicines began a phase 3 trial of GB-0895 on 2025-12-03, an antibody engineered with its generative platform. The data does not include any result from that trial.

Do higher hit rates mean lower development costs?

The data does not hold this. It supports the narrower claim that fewer wet lab cycles are needed per candidate, because more of the proposed designs bind. Cost of development after design is not covered.

explainer:
Traditional antibody discovery immunises animals or screens large libraries, then optimises the best hits through rounds of laboratory engineering. Generative design works the other way: a model is given a target and proposes antibody or protein sequences predicted to bind it, sometimes with required properties such as stability or low immunogenicity built in. De novo design means creating binders with no starting antibody at all.

The appeal is speed and reach. Generative models can propose binders for targets that are hard to hit with conventional methods and can explore far more designs than a lab could test. Companies report much higher experimental hit rates than random screening, and the first generatively engineered antibodies have entered late stage trials. The caveats are that reported hit rates come mostly from the companies themselves, depend heavily on the target, and say nothing about whether a binder becomes a safe, manufacturable medicine, which still takes conventional development.

What generative design means for proteins

Antibodies and other therapeutic proteins have traditionally been found rather than designed: by immunising animals, by screening large libraries, or by evolving candidates in the laboratory. Generative models change the starting point. Given a target and the properties wanted, such as binding strength, stability, manufacturability and low immune reaction risk, a model proposes sequences expected to have them, and the laboratory tests the proposals rather than searching from scratch.

What has been achieved

Designed proteins that bind chosen targets have been confirmed experimentally in many studies, and designed enzymes and binders have been made that do not exist in nature. For antibodies, which are large and complex, full design from sequence is harder than for smaller proteins, but models now improve existing antibodies, propose variants with better properties and reduce the number of rounds of laboratory optimisation. Several companies have therapeutic candidates from these methods in early trials.

What still decides success

A model proposes; the laboratory decides. Expression yield, stability in a vial, behaviour in the body and immune reactions are tested the hard way, and many promising designs fail there. The companies ahead in this area pair generative models with high throughput experiments that feed results back into the models, so that each round of design learns from the last. Regulators treat a designed protein like any other biologic: the method of discovery does not change the evidence required, though it may change how much of the early data a sponsor is asked to explain.
